entries.test: Contemporaneous industry statements, reporting, and market reactions would show whether DeepSeek alarmed the American AI industry over costs rather than national security.
entries.note: This asserts a cause of an industry reaction that public evidence can assess.

entries.test: Microsoft's documented data center cancellations and contemporaneous AI investment and valuation trends would show whether those withdrawals signaled an emerging contraction.
entries.note: The plain reading is an early contraction in the AI investment boom.
The surrounding paragraph supplies the company description, but 'time bomb' specifies no concrete failure.

entries.test: Generative AI companies' financial statements would establish whether any was profitable at the time of the claim.
entries.note: A single profitable generative AI company would refute the universal claim.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and independent evaluations of systems autonomously executing delegated tasks would establish whether functioning AI agents exist.
entries.note: The impossibility assertion is also refutable by a working example; product branding alone is insufficient.
'No AI SaaS story' does not unambiguously mean no viable business. The industry's 'fate' and its dependence on GPU sales have no shared operational threshold here.

entries.test: Public acquisition and IPO records, valuations, and financial disclosures would show whether the described AI companies can achieve exits despite their valuations and business economics.
entries.note: The assertion of impossibility is firm and can be contradicted by completed transactions.

entries.test: Data center developer acquisition and listing records, together with national accounts decomposing US economic growth, would test both assertions.
entries.note: This bundles two independently testable claims; 'entirely' makes the growth assertion particularly strong.

entries.test: Public estimates of OpenAI's funding requirements and worldwide available financial resources would test the asserted funding shortfall.
entries.note: The source says funding OpenAI generally, not specifically funding its commitments. It presents the claim as a fact, allowing a literal financial test.

entries.test: GPU shipment, inventory, and deployment disclosures would establish whether millions remained uninstalled, while financing disclosures would test dependence on continuing debt.
entries.note: This mixes factual assertions with a judgment against buying more GPUs, so observation alone is inadequate. The factual components are checkable; the recommendation is a value judgment.
'Threatens the future' specifies neither a financial outcome nor a threshold for harm across these institutions.

entries.test: OpenAI's cumulative revenue through September 2025 and the cited first-half revenue reports would settle the numerical discrepancy.
entries.note: The normalization adds a claim about what first-half reports implied; the source only calls the figures vastly different.

entries.test: Cumulative AI revenue attributable to the GPU purchases under discussion, compared with their acquisition costs, would establish whether those costs are ever recovered.
entries.note: 'These GPUs' refers to the purchases under discussion, whereas the normalization generalizes to NVIDIA GPUs.
The warehouse assertion is explicitly qualified by 'likely.' The separate categorical denial of six million installed Blackwell GPUs is checkable and should be split out.

entries.test: Public inference-cost measurements or infrastructure billing disclosures comparing GPT-5 router mode with comparable direct model use would test the claimed additional running cost.
entries.note: The ordinary reading is that routing adds operating costs rather than achieving savings.

entries.test: OpenAI's cash-flow and financing disclosures compared with previously published cash-burn estimates for the same period would establish whether the gap exceeded $4 billion.
entries.note: The article title and surrounding description support reading 'we know' as previously public knowledge.

entries.test: OpenAI's financial resources and contractual payment schedule, alongside Oracle's available and committed compute capacity as of September 12, 2025, would test the asserted inability to fulfill the deal.
entries.note: The source dates its finding to September 12; the normalization shifts that historical assessment into an unqualified present claim.

entries.test: The payment obligations and infrastructure costs in OpenAI's agreed deals as of September 26, 2025, would establish whether executing them required at least $1 trillion over the following four years.
entries.note: The four-year window is anchored to the September analysis, not the retrospective's publication. This is a claim about existing funding requirements, so assessment need not await the window's end.
The normalization adds an abrupt reversal absent from the source. 'Everybody' treating AI as uniquely special until accepting otherwise supplies no agreed behavioral test.
